USDA Forest Service Office/Lab and Location: A fellowship opportunity is available with the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service (FS) within the Forest Service Northern Research Station (NRS) located in Grand Rapids, Minnesota. Grand Rapids is a small, rural community in north-central Minnesota. The Forestry Sciences Laboratory is located on the University of Minnesota North Central Research and Outreach Center adjacent to the Minnesota North Community College - Itasca Campus. 

Grand Rapids is located among the forests, lakes, and headwater streams of the Mississippi River in rural, north-central Minnesota. The Northern Research Forestry Sciences Laboratory supports forest, ecology, aquatics, and hydrological research throughout the region, including research at the Marcell, Cutfoot, and Pike Bay Experimental Forests. The participant will report in-person to the facility up to 5 days a week, with no possibility for remote participation. The chemistry laboratory in the Grand Rapids Forestry Sciences Laboratory supports studies of forest and resource management. The office is part of the Research and Development mission area of the USDA Forest Service. In addition to research of NRS scientists, the laboratory supports analysis for the NRS Forest Inventory and Analysis Program, other cooperating federal agencies, and academic partners.

At the heart of the USDA Forest Service's mission is their purpose. Everything they do is intended to help sustain forests and grasslands for present and future generations. Why? Because their stewardship work supports nature in sustaining life. This is the purpose that drives the agency’s mission and motivates their work across the agency. It’s been there from the agency’s very beginning, and it still drives them. To advance the mission and serve their purpose, the USDA Forest Service balances the short and long-term needs of people and nature by: working in collaboration with communities and our partners; providing access to resources and experiences that promote economic, ecological, and social vitality; connecting people to the land and one another; and delivering world-class science, technology and land management.

Research Project: Fellows will gain awareness of a range of activities associated with a chemistry laboratory. Fellows will gain perspective on and experience how soil samples are prepared for chemical analysis. Samples may be soil, sediment, plant tissue, or water collected from studies. Mentored by a research scientist serving as project leader, fellows will train on laboratory techniques and equipment used by a laboratory manager (chemist), a physical sciences technician, and other staff. Through these interactions, fellows will have time to see how and why samples are prepared for chemical analysis. Forest Service staff will share through discussions and hands-on training how science support positions contribute to research in government agencies and academia. Secondary opportunities may include gaining knowledge and experience in field research associated with watershed and forest ecology studies including physical and biological measurements or sample collection.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will have the opportunity to learn to:

Understand how and why samples are prepared for chemical analysis and apply that knowledge.

Gain familiarity with the laboratory techniques and equipment used to prepare samples for chemical analysis.

Develop laboratory skills and gain exposure to research and research operations that support the mission of Forest Service Research and Development.

Gain understanding and how science support positions contribute to research in government agencies and academia.

There may be opportunities, including field activities, to shadow Forest Service and cooperating science support staff while participating in other research that is based out of the office. 

Mentor: The mentor for this opportunity is Stephen Sebestyen ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: 2026.  Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year but may be extended upon recommendation of USDA Forest Service and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The fellowship is expected to at a partial level of participation. The duration of the appointment is flexible, with a minimum expectation of about a semester. If extended over the summer, there may be opportunity to participate at a higher level of participation.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. Anticipated stipend range is $680 - $1,360 monthly.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens, Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR), and foreign nationals. Non-U.S. citizen applicants should refer to the Guidelines for Non-U.S. Citizens Details page of the program website for information about the valid immigration statuses that are acceptable for program participation. Foreign national candidates may have a mandatory in-person requirement depending on visa status.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and USDA Forest Service. Participants do not become employees of USDA, USDA Forest Service, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Wyndmoor, Pennsylvania.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The Sustainable Biofuels and Co-Products Research Unit (SBCP) in Wyndmoor, PA, develops technologies that support new markets and increased profitability for U.S. agriculture. Researchers in SBCP advance chemical, catalytic, thermal, enzymatic, and fermentative technologies to convert low-value agricultural materials into high-value products such as biofuels, renewable chemicals and materials.

Research Project: This research project aims to improve the utilization of herbaceous feedstocks by extracting, characterizing, and utilizing lignin for bio-based material applications. The project involves fractionating lignin out of lignocellulosic biomass (e.g. switchgrass and hemp) using chemical pretreatment followed by downstream recovery of the dissolved lignin. The recovered lignin will be characterized for physico-chemical properties and be utilized in research to prepare bio-based materials. You will participate in this research by helping conduct lignin fractionation experiments, perform analytical characterization of the recovered lignin, and prepare bio-based materials using the recovered lignin.

Learning Objectives: You will gain experience, in a research setting, by assisting with lignin fractionation experiments to include recording data, analyzing and summarizing data, preparing scientific reports, and presenting research progress during group meetings. You will also gain hands-on experience with a variety of analytical techniques such as HPLC, TGA, NMR, and FTIR.

During the appointment, You will:

Increase knowledge in chemical and biological biomass conversion technologies and plant cell wall chemistry.
Develop skills in statistical design of experiments.
Gain experience with analytical techniques that support characterization of biomass and biomass conversion products.
Learn how to collect, organize and process data from analytical instruments and experimental analyses.
Enhance scientific communication skills by assisting with the preparation of detailed scientific reports and presenting research progress to the research unit.

Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email [email removed]  and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Description
GRADUATE RESEARCH OPPORTUNITY (MS or PhD) to study the breeding ecology and nesting behavior of the Painted Bunting (Passerina ciris) in north Texas. The student along with faculty collaborators will continue a long-term study on a breeding population of Painted Buntings. Over 500 Painted Buntings have been uniquely color banded at a ~40-ha study area near the University of North Texas campus since 2017. Birds exhibit annual site fidelity, and modeling has produced annual survival estimates of 60-80%. The specific research direction is open, but questions related to breeding ecology, nesting behavior, habitat selection and use, delayed plumage maturation, migration movement ecology, population demography and trends, and conservation needs could be further addressed. The student will be encouraged to propose research questions that could be answered by using data from a long-term marked population of songbirds. The data collection will likely involve capturing and marking birds with color bands, monitoring survival and site fidelity, possibly using telemetry devices, and locating and monitoring nests depending on the research questions selected. 
 Applicants should have a strong interest in animal and behavioral ecology, as well as conservation. Candidates that have completed MS research and published on avian ecology/conservation topics will receive preference. The student will be expected to collect field data in the late-spring and summer period (May – August) in north Texas. The student would be required to qualify for a Teaching Assistantship during fall and spring semesters in the Department of Biological Sciences.
 Starting graduate stipend is estimated at $24,200/year plus waiver of most fees and tuition. A student heath insurance plan is available for PhD students.
 The selected applicant will begin field work during the spring/summer 2028. Course work will begin in August 2027. Please send letter of interest including suggested research ideas/questions that could be addressed by studying a marked population of songbirds, C.V. (or resume), and unofficial copies of transcripts (B.S. and M.S) to JIM BEDNARZ ([email removed]), Dept. of Biological Sciences, University of North Texas. ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity focused on the development of novel detection methods for foodborne pathogenic bacteria is available at the USDA, Agricultural Research Service, Eastern Regional Research Center, Characterization and Interventions for Foodborne Pathogens (CIFP) Research Unit in Wyndmoor, Pennsylvania.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The mission of the CIFP research unit is to investigate multiple areas of safety-related problems associated with contamination of food by bacterial pathogens and includes: stress response, evolution/mutation, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, intervention techniques, and rapid detection & identification. The research project in this subgroup focuses on the stress responses for specific foodborne pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes). Analysis is typically complicated by the complex nature of food matrices and the frequent need to develop virulence assays using different mammalian cell lines.

During the appointment, you will assist in research and development focused on one or more advanced areas of interest (e.g., molecular microbiology and biochemistry). This research will complement your academic education with the application of:

BSL2 pathogen handling
Genome sequencing, transcriptomics
Bioinformatic analysis, Computational biology
Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn about food-safety research focused on bacterial contamination and foodborne pathogens.
Develop knowledge of stress-response mechanisms in pathogens such as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella, and Listeria monocytogenes.
Gain experience investigating pathogen evolution and mutation, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence.
Learn how food-matrix complexity affects the detection, characterization, and analysis of foodborne bacteria.
Build skills in developing and conducting virulence assays using mammalian cell lines.
Strengthen laboratory research, experimental-design, and data-analysis skills relevant to microbial food-safety studies.

Description
 The Qiu Lab at Duke University is recruiting one fully funded Ph.D. student to begin in Fall 2027 (application deadline: December 1, 2026). Our research aims to understand and predict changes in biodiversity and ecosystem functioning across spatial and temporal scales. The student will develop an independent research direction within or across the themes below, with opportunities to contribute to ongoing projects supported by NASA, NSF, and private foundations. Learn more about our ongoing research projects and future research directions at www.tongqiulab.com. 


Research Directions

1.  Ecological remote sensing for forest and savanna ecosystems. Characterize and understand the spatial and temporal variation in the structure, functioning, and dynamics of forests and savannas. Integrate emerging remote sensing technologies, including imaging spectroscopy, LiDAR, and satellite-based time series, to investigate ecosystem responses to environmental change. 

2. Biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. Investigate how interactions between plants and wildlife shape ecosystem processes, including carbon and nutrient cycling. Combine remote sensing, field inventories, wildlife monitoring, and statistical models to understand how fire, grazing, and the reintroduction of large herbivores (e.g., rhinos and elephants) influence biodiversity and its contributions to ecosystem functioning. 

3. AI for Ecology. Develop and apply advanced AI methods, including deep learning and foundation models, to uncover ecological patterns and improve ecological predictions using large-scale Earth observation data and long-term ecological monitoring datasets. 


Preferred Candidate Expertise 

Backgrounds in ecology, environmental science, remote sensing, geography, statistics, computer science, or related fields are welcome. Preferred qualifications include: 

•  Experience with LiDAR, hyperspectral data, statistical ecology, or machine/deep learning. 

•  Experience with R and/or Python and quantitative/statistical analysis 

•  Research initiative, intellectual curiosity, willingness to learn, and a collaborative mindset. 


Lab Resources 

Remote Sensing Equipment:  RIEGL VZ-400i Terrestrial Laser Scanner; NaturaSpec UV–Vis–NIR–SWIR field spectroradiometers; HySpex airborne hyperspectral imaging system. Computing:  individual research workstations and access to high-performance computing clusters and GPU resources. 


How to Apply 

Formal applications:  Apply to Duke’s Ph.D. in Environment or University Program in Ecology (UPE), depending on your research interests. Ecology emphasizes biodiversity and ecological processes; Environment also accommodates environmental remote sensing and interdisciplinary work. For Fall 2027 admission, the Ecology deadline is December 1, 2026, and the Environment deadline is December 3, 2026. 

Initial inquiry:  Email [email removed] with subject “application for PhD 2027 – [Your Name]”. Please provide: 

•  Your current CV and undergraduate/graduate transcripts (as applicable). 

•  An approximately one-page statement describing previous research, questions you hope to pursue, and why the Qiu Lab is a good fit. 

•  A research paper or writing sample, if available. 

•  Names and contact information for three potential references. 

Contact
Tong Qiu

Description: We seek a motivated doctoral student to join the Christensen Lab in the Department of Fisheries and Wildlife at Michigan State University. The successful applicant will conduct research evaluating deer population responses to community-based deer management interventions in Michigan. This position is funded through a doctoral research assistantship for the four-year project period (January 2027 through September 2030). The selected candidate will work with a team of collaborators from Michigan State University and the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, and will contribute to the multi-state effort of the CWD Research Consortium.
 Project Description: This position is part of Evaluating New Approaches to Deer Overabundance and Chronic Wasting Disease Management, a broader four-year project led by Michigan State University (MSU) in partnership with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR) Wildlife Division. The project tests whether coordinated, community-based deer management interventions can increase hunter harvest and change deer population and disease outcomes, using a treatment and control design in townships in the southern Lower Peninsula of Michigan. It contributes to a multi-state effort evaluating approaches to deer management in CWD-affected areas across the Midwest. The broad project combines assessments of hunter and landowner social and behavioral conditions with ecological outcomes such as deer harvest, density, demographics, and CWD prevalence. The project team includes Dr. Sonja Christensen (ecological and disease components) and Dr. Emily Pomeranz (human dimensions) of the MSU Department of Fisheries and Wildlife, and Dr. Dwayne Etter and Dr. Brent Rudolph of the Michigan DNR Wildlife Division. Dr. Sonja Christensen and the selected PhD student will focus on the ecological and disease components of the project. 
 Research Objective: Determine whether management interventions produce changes in hunter behavior and deer harvest, and result in associated changes in deer density, population demographics, and CWD prevalence, by comparing treatment and control townships before and after interventions.
 Responsibilities: The selected Doctoral Research Assistant will be responsible for:
Using baseline and follow-up assessments of deer populations, including roadside distance sampling, to estimate deer density in an experimental study.
Evaluating changes in deer harvest (with an emphasis on antlerless deer), density, demographics, fawn recruitment, and CWD prevalence in treatment and control townships.
Developing models and statistical analyses to address the research objectives, including the effects of interventions and other factors (e.g., epizootic hemorrhagic disease events) on deer populations.
Collaborating with a multidisciplinary team of ecologists, social scientists, and agency partners, including the Michigan DNR and the MSU Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory.
Contributing to community engagement with landowners, hunters, and other stakeholders.
Preparing research findings for publication in peer-reviewed journals, presenting results at conferences, and communicating findings to state wildlife agencies and the public.
 Qualifications:
A master’s degree in a relevant field (e.g., wildlife biology, epidemiology, ecology, statistics, or related field). 
Experience with wildlife population estimation methods (e.g., distance sampling) preferred.
Strong quantitative and analytical skills/aptitude.
Experience with statistical software preferred (e.g., R, SAS, Python).
Excellent communication skills, both written and oral.
Ability to work independently and as part of a collaborative, interdisciplinary team.
Interest in working with stakeholders and communities.
Passion for wildlife conservation, management, and research.
Experience working with state wildlife agencies and engagement with hunting populations is preferred.
 Program Support: The selected Doctoral Research Assistant will receive:
Full tuition remission, health benefits, and a bi-weekly stipend (see below); supported for the four-year project period, one semester of TA expected).
Opportunities for professional development and networking.

Applications: Interested candidates should submit the following materials to Dr. Sonja Christensen ([email removed]). IMPORTANT: Submit applications with “PhD Application: Wildlife Estimation and Health” in the subject line (single merged PDF file is preferred):
A cover letter outlining your research interests and career goals.
A resume or curriculum vitae.
GRE scores preferred but not required
TOEFL scores (for non-native English speakers only).
Academic transcripts (unofficial copies are acceptable at this stage).
Contact information for three references.
One representative first-authored publication if any exist. 
 Application Deadline: Review of applications will begin immediately and the final deadline for submission is October 30th, 2026.
 Salary and Start Date: Minimum annual stipend of $34,789, plus tuition covered and health benefits, and annual 3% raises. Some stipend flexibility available based on experience and degrees. Start date is January 2027. Funding is budgeted through the end of the project in September 2030 with options for Teaching Assistantships or Fellowships for the remaining academic program assuming positive academic progress. 
Contact Information: For inquiries about the position or the research project, please contact Dr. Sonja Christensen ([email removed]) or reach out to members of my lab. Please allow time for email response. 

More about The Christensen Lab: Join our team at the Christensen Lab and contribute to critical research that addresses the challenges posed by CWD and its impact on ungulate populations. We look forward to welcoming a dedicated PhD student to our project and our dynamic research group. Our lab focuses on evaluations of wildlife population health and understanding the dynamics of infectious diseases in wildlife populations to develop strategies for their management and conservation. We employ cutting-edge field research, quantitative modeling, and interdisciplinary approaches to address critical challenges in wildlife health. For more information about our lab, please visit our website: www.christensen-lab.org. Further, Michigan State University’s Department of Fisheries and Wildlife is one of the largest programs of its kind, with 45 core faculty (http://canr.msu.edu/fw).

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: Due to the large number of chemicals in commerce and subsequently introduced into the environment, chemical safety assessments reliant on traditional animal testing have been unable to keep pace with the need to generate hazard and exposure data to support screening, prioritization, and human health risk assessment. To address this, EPA's Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention is developing and evaluating in vitro-based "New Approach Method" (NAM) testing strategies to rapidly and cost-effectively inform such decision-making. EPA's Risk Assessment Support Division is developing and applying high throughput test methods to identify NAM-based in vitro points of departure - concentrations at which biological perturbations are observed. Exposure-dose modeling leverages chemical-specific toxicokinetic data to estimate what external exposures are required to achieve systemic blood concentrations that are equivalent to these assay-derived in vitro points of departure. By incorporating NAM data into a model that recapitulates "real-world", in vivo exposure scenarios, the NAM data can be directly translated into "equivalent doses," which can then be compared to anticipated exposure levels to evaluate risk (hazard + exposure = risk). The toxicokinetic data are generated using cell-based or biochemical assays combined with analytical chemistry techniques to characterize changes in chemical concentrations. 

With guidance from the mentor, you may be involved in any or all of the following training activities:

Conducting cell-based and/or biochemical assays that measure chemical absorption, plasma binding, metabolism and other in vitro toxicokinetic/toxicodynamic endpoints.
Extracting and preparing assay samples for analysis by a range of mass spectrometry methods.
Developing customized analytical methods to evaluate a wide range of commercial chemicals or emerging contaminants, by tandem mass spectrometry coupled with either gas or liquid chromatographic separation. 
Analyzing experimental data and generating tables, figures, and other summaries of results.
Applying quality assurance/quality control principles, statistical analyses, and computational models to interpret data sets and to implement in vitro-in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) exposure-dose modeling. 
Compiling and summarizing scientific information from the peer-reviewed literature and from on-line data sources.
Presenting research results at internal and/or scientific meetings and contributing to peer-reviewed publications.
Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn a wide range of laboratory techniques which can be applied across several life sciences and analytical chemistry research disciplines. You will learn to operate and use a range of scientific equipment. You will learn to execute cellular and/or biochemical assays. You will learn search strategies and tools to efficiently and transparently document literature retrieval and evaluation. You will learn to evaluate data quality, troubleshoot research results, and apply statistical methods for data analysis and interpretation.

You will be integrated into a multidisciplinary research team and engaged in multiple aspects of project planning, communication, research implementation, and analysis. You will be afforded an opportunity to interact with internationally recognized leaders, both within and outside EPA. You will have the opportunity to contribute to original research and associated publications. It is expected that this training opportunity will provide you with knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to apply new technologies and associated data to regulatory decision-making at the local, national, and/or international scale and to a professional career in life sciences research.

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Barbara Wetmore ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: Fall/Winter 2026. All start dates are flexible and vary depending on numerous factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year and may be renewed three to four additional years upon EPA recommendation and subject to availability of funding.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens and Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR) only.

EPA Security Clearance: Completion of a successful background investigation by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is required for an applicant to be on-boarded at EPA.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and EPA. Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5-year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility.

Questions: Please see the FAQ section of our website. If you have additional questions about the application process please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a bachelor's or master's degree in the one of the relevant fields (biology, toxicology, chemistry, biochemistry, molecular biology, cellular biology, bioinformatics, computational toxicology, or a related field). Degree must have been received within the past five years, or be currently pursuing.

Degree preference is a received bachelor's, or pursuing or received master's.

 Description: We seek a motivated master’s student to join the Christensen Lab in the Department of Fisheries and Wildlife at Michigan State University. The successful applicant will conduct research on standardized roadside distance sampling for estimating white-tailed deer density in areas managed for chronic wasting disease (CWD). This position is funded through a research assistantship on a USDA-funded project. The selected candidate will work with a team of collaborators from Michigan State University, state wildlife agencies, and USDA partners. 
 Project Description: This position is part of Standardizing Deer Density Estimation to Support Multi-State Evaluation of CWD and White-Tailed Deer Management, a USDA-funded project led by Michigan State University (MSU). The project will use data from standardized roadside distance sampling surveys in 24 paired treatment and control units across Michigan, Missouri, Ohio, and Wisconsin to establish baseline deer density estimates and will develop the protocols, training materials, and centralized data infrastructure needed to evaluate deer population responses to management over time among Midwest states. This project is in conjunction with a broader effort by the CWD Research Consortium’s Objective 4 adaptive management project and builds on earlier USDA-supported MSU research that evaluated methods for estimating white-tailed deer density. In Michigan, the work is coordinated with complementary projects in the same units, including the MSU and Michigan DNR project Evaluating New Approaches to Deer Overabundance and CWD Management. Collaborators include the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, Missouri Department of Conservation, Ohio Division of Wildlife, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, the Montana Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit, and the USDA APHIS National Wildlife Research Center. 
 Research Objective: Generate standardized estimates of deer density from roadside distance sampling within paired treatment and control units, and evaluate how these estimates compare with other density estimation approaches (e.g., camera surveys, drone surveys, and harvest-based estimates) where overlapping data are available. Scale our estimation recommendations to township-level assessments for regional state wildlife agencies and develop a centralized data infrastructure for multi-state comparisons. 
 Responsibilities: The selected Master’s Research Assistant will be responsible for: 
Conducting standardized roadside distance sampling surveys within Michigan treatment and control units (approximately 36 square miles each).
Contributing to survey protocols, observer training materials, and quality assurance procedures used across participating states.
Communicating with state agency partners and research collaborators in a timely and professional manner. 
Analyzing survey data using distance sampling methods to estimate detection functions and deer density with associated measures of precision.
Comparing roadside distance sampling estimates with other available density datasets.
Contributing to centralized data management and the integration of density estimates with harvest, human dimensions, and CWD surveillance data.
Collaborating with agency partners in Michigan, Missouri, Ohio, and Wisconsin.
Preparing a thesis and manuscripts for publication, and presenting results at conferences.

 

Qualifications:
 A bachelor’s degree in a relevant field (e.g., wildlife biology, ecology, epidemiology, statistics, or related field).
Experience with distance sampling or other wildlife population survey methods preferred.
Strong quantitative and analytical skills/aptitude.
Experience with statistical software preferred (e.g., R, Python).
Excellent communication skills, both written and oral.
Ability to work independently and as part of a collaborative research team.
Passion for wildlife conservation, management, and research.
Experience working with state wildlife agencies is preferred.

 

Program Support: The selected Master’s Research Assistant will receive:
 Full tuition remission, health benefits, and a bi-weekly stipend (see below) for two years, one semester of Teaching Assistantship may be possible.

 

Applications: Interested candidates should submit the following materials to Dr. Sonja Christensen ([email removed]). IMPORTANT: Submit applications with “MS Application: Wildlife Estimation and Health” in the subject line (single merged PDF file is preferred):
 A cover letter outlining your research interests and goals.
A resume or curriculum vitae.
GRE scores preferred but not required
TOEFL scores (for non-native English speakers only).
Academic transcripts (unofficial copies are acceptable at this stage).
Contact information for three references.
One representative first-authored publication or report if one exists.

 

Application Deadline: Review of applications will begin immediately and the final deadline for submission is October 30th, 2026.



Salary and Start Date: Minimum annual stipend starting at $33,276, plus tuition and health benefits. Start date is January 2027. Funding is available for 2 years, and the option to TA to cover an additional semester may be considered if the student is in good academic standing.

Contact Information: For inquiries about the position or the research project, please contact Dr. Sonja Christensen ([email removed]) or reach out to members of my lab. Please allow time for email response.

More about the Christensen Lab: Join our team at the Christensen Lab and contribute to critical research that addresses the challenges posed by high-density deer populations, CWD, and its impact on wildlife population health. We look forward to welcoming a dedicated MS student to our project and our dynamic research group. Our lab focuses on evaluations of wildlife population health and understanding the dynamics of infectious diseases in wildlife populations to develop strategies for their management and conservation. We employ cutting-edge field research, quantitative modeling, and interdisciplinary approaches to address critical challenges in wildlife health. For more information about our lab, please visit our website: www.christensen-lab.org. Further, Michigan State University’s Department of Fisheries and Wildlife is one of the largest programs of its kind, with 45 core faculty (http://canr.msu.edu/fw).

POSITION AND RESPONSIBILITIES: The Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources at the University of Georgia invites applications for a tenure-track faculty position in forest productivity and management at the Assistant or Associate Professor level, with outreach, research, and university and professional service expectations as part of a 9-month appointment. The position includes two additional months of renewable summer salary, consistent with faculty holding majority outreach appointments, with the opportunity to earn additional summer salary through extramural funding. This position is located at the Bulloch County Extension Office in Statesboro, Georgia, and is an off-campus appointment; occasional travel to Athens and elsewhere in the state and region will be required. Successful candidates will be expected to establish interdisciplinary collaborations in outreach and research with faculty in the Warnell School and across the UGA campus. Individuals with expertise in forest productivity, forest economics, silviculture, prescribed fire, forest management, forest soils, or a closely related discipline are encouraged to apply, with particular interest in programming that serves non-industrial private landowners.

Outreach responsibilities (70%) should be satisfied by developing educational activities, publications, and programs (a series of related activities building to develop competencies) which address the needs or requests of non-industrial private landowners, forest industry professionals, state and federal agencies, non-governmental organizations, and county extension personnel in Georgia and beyond. Excellence in outreach programming should involve using creative and innovative delivery strategies (face-to-face, online, video-based, podcasts, etc.) for reaching groups, along with individual, one-on-one consultations for technical assistance related to forest productivity and management.

Research responsibilities (25%) include development of an externally funded, regionally/nationally recognized program in forest productivity and management (e.g., intensive pine silviculture, forest fertilization and site productivity, forest soils and nutrition management, stand density and thinning economic decisions, regeneration and establishment, vegetation management, pine straw management, prescribed fire, etc.). Research and outreach programming/publications may be directly linked. Consultation and technical assistance will be defined as providing specialized knowledge to stakeholders within the scope of the Warnell School mission. The successful candidate will interact with and advise non-industrial private landowners, industry professionals, state and federal agencies, non-profit organizations, and extension professionals. 

Professional Service (5%) includes serving on School/University committees and actively participating in professional/scientific societies among other like activities.

QUALIFICATIONS: Required—Candidates must possess a Ph.D. with an emphasis on forest productivity, silviculture, forest management, or a closely related natural resource discipline (e.g., biometrics, natural resource management and sustainability, water and soil resources), with at least one degree (B.S., M.S., or Ph.D.) in forest resource management or a closely related discipline and strong academic performance in core coursework as reflected on college transcripts; ABD candidates are encouraged to apply, with the expectation that the degree will be completed prior to the position start date. Candidates must demonstrate clear evidence of scholarship through peer-reviewed publications and/or technical publications, and the ability to attract extramural funding. Candidates must have authored or coauthored a journal article, proceedings paper, or scientific presentation. The successful candidate will demonstrate potential for outreach productivity, a clear understanding of the outreach mission as reflected in the required outreach and research statement and should have interest in outreach education and conducting and reporting research relevant to non-industrial private landowners. The candidate must also demonstrate potential and willingness to work closely with public and private partners, outreach professionals, and other constituent groups, and be able to successfully mentor students. 

Preferred—Candidates who have developed and published outreach products (e.g., outreach publications, fact sheets, videos, podcasts) or delivered outreach presentations. Candidates who have worked or completed field work related to undergraduate or graduate degree requirements in the southeastern United States or who have worked in the region as a seasonal or full-time forestry technician, field forester, forestry consultant, or land manager. Candidates who have produced and published (as an author, rather than solely contributed to) a journal article, proceedings paper, or scientific presentation from a research project. Candidates who have the potential or have shown the ability to use modern, innovative outreach tools. Candidates who can integrate science and stakeholder values into their research program. Candidates whose research addresses forest productivity challenges affecting non-industrial private landowners at regional or larger spatial scales and demonstrate an ability to translate research into outcomes relevant to appropriate audiences.

ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS: Appointment to Associate Professor requires a record consistent with promotion to Associate Professor at the Warnell School such as strong evidence of emerging stature as a regional/national authority, acquiring and administering external funding, ability to produce and communicate research, and excellence in outreach and working with stakeholders. Service at the Associate Professor level for 1-2 years is preferred for this rank.

THE UNIVERSITY: The University of Georgia (www.uga.edu) is a top 20 ranked public land/sea/space grant institution comprised of 18 schools and colleges and designated as a Carnegie Very High Research Activity (R1) institution with strong community engagement. Athens is a diverse community of approximately 150,000 people located less than 75 miles from Atlanta. UGA enrolls approximately 41,200 undergraduate, graduate, and professional students. The Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources is a professional school with world class research, teaching, and outreach programs in natural resources conservation and is committed to inclusive excellence. The Warnell School is comprised of 70 faculty, 100 support staff, 265 undergraduates, and 240 graduate students (www.warnell.uga.edu). The school offers Bachelor of Science, Master of Forest Resources, Master of Natural Resources, Master of Science, and Doctor of Philosophy degrees in the areas of Forestry; Fisheries & Wildlife; Parks, Recreation & Tourism Management; and Natural Resource Management & Sustainability. The school manages over 17,000 acres of forestland across the state in support of its teaching, outreach, and research missions. This position will be based at the Bulloch County Extension Office in Statesboro, Georgia, serving non-industrial private landowners and stakeholders across the region.

APPLICATION: To ensure full consideration, candidates must submit a cover letter, curriculum vitae, statement of outreach and research interests, including strategies for obtaining external funding for research programs (statements totaling less than three pages), unofficial transcripts of all college-level work, copies of up to three recent publications, and contact information for three references by November 15, 2026. Individuals selected as finalists will be asked to submit official college transcripts to [email removed]. Letters of reference will be solicited by the search chair for finalists prior to interviews. Finalists will be required to provide a signed consent form authorizing the University to conduct a background check (www.hr.uga.edu). The background investigation will be conducted on a post-offer/pre-employment basis. The start date is August 1, 2027, but is negotiable. All applicants must apply online through the University of Georgia Faculty Jobs system (https://www.ugajobsearch.com/postings/508273). No paper applications will be accepted. For additional information, please contact Dr. David Clabo, Chair, Forest Productivity and Management Search Committee ([email removed]).

The University of Georgia is an Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action employer. All qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, ethnicity, age, genetic information, disability, gender identity, sexual orientation or protected veteran status. Persons needing accommodations or assistance with the accessibility of materials related to this search are encouraged to contact Central HR ([email removed]). Please do not contact the department or search committee with such requests.
Contact
David Clabo

You will be a part of a multi-year project aimed at:

Characterizing fungal population structure and succession across key phenological stages of corn.
Applying molecular and microbiome sequencing approaches (e.g., ITS/TEF amplicon sequencing, qPCR, metagenomics) to track fungal communities.

Description
Open Rank Professor of Applied Waterfowl and Wetland Ecology
School of Environment and Natural Resources
College of Food, Agricultural, and Environmental Sciences
The Ohio State University

This is a full-time 9-month tenure-track appointment with responsibilities distributed as described across research, teaching and service. Our aim is to recruit, support, and retain a scholar that will foster science based conservation of migratory waterfowl and other gamebirds, as well as wetlands and associated upland habitats that sustain wildlife populations and human well-being. Pending Board of Trustee approval, this position will include annual research funds and an Endowed Professorship for those at appropriate rank supported by Winous Point Marsh Conservancy (WPMC). WPMC is committed to providing additional research funding, facilities and logistical support for this research program consistent with their mission.

We encourage applications from scholars with an emphasis on the generation, dissemination, and application of science-based knowledge to inform conservation and management decisions. We strongly encourage applications whose scholarship demonstrates an integrated program in wildlife ecology and conservation with emphasis on:
Population dynamics of waterfowl and other bird species
Ecology and management of wetlands and associated upland systems
Wetland habitat restoration and ecosystem services
Interactions among ecological function, wildlife conservation, and human use

The successful candidate will teach approximately 2 undergraduate or graduate courses per year, primarily in waterfowl and wetlands ecology, wildlife population management, and experiential learning courses. They will collaborate with SENR faculty, Ohio State University Extension and SeaGrant, the Ohio Department of Natural Resources Division of Wildlife, the Winous Point Marsh Conservancy, and other partners on applied research and outreach opportunities. Depending on experience and qualifications, the incumbent may have a significant co-leadership or coordinating role in the Terrestrial Wildlife Ecology Laboratory conducting and administering grant-funded research, education and outreach programs.

Performance Objectives
1. Develop new or enhance existing courses aligned with SENR’s Forestry, Fisheries and Wildlife major.
2. Demonstrate an ability to cultivate learning environments where students feel they belong within the School of Environment and Natural Resources and related professions.
3. Contribute to professional development and outreach workshops for practitioners and stakeholders.
4. Engage with and provide leadership for the Terrestrial Wildlife Ecology Laboratory.
5. Develop and/or expand an independent research program on the ecology and management of waterfowl, wetlands, and associated wildlife communities, including presenting results at national and international meetings, securing extramural funding, and producing impactful publications.
6. Advise graduate and undergraduate students, including Environment and Natural Resources Graduate Program and SENR honors students.
7. Work collaboratively with university faculty and staff, School of Environment and Natural Resources and/or OSU extension, government agencies, non-government organizations, and/or community groups to advance the land grant mission of the college and university.
8. Serve the School of Environment and Natural Resources, university, and professional communities through committee work and other appropriate activities, including serving as faculty advisor for student organizations such as Ducks Unlimited.

Education and Experience Requirements
Required:
Earned Ph.D. in wildlife ecology, wetlands science, or a closely related field
Demonstrated interest in or experience with applied research on wildlife populations and habitat ecology in wetland systems
Experience conducting field-based studies and ecological investigations
Strong quantitative and analytical skills
Evidence of potential for excellence in research and teaching.
Excellent verbal and written communication skills and a willingness and ability to work closely with diverse groups of academic (e.g., students, staff, faculty) and practitioner audiences.
Demonstrated interest in and/or experience with teaching, recruiting, mentoring, and advising a diverse body of students.

Desired:
Experience integrating research, teaching, and outreach
Evidence of interdisciplinary collaboration, with environmental and social scientists
Experience securing external funding
Engagement with stakeholders, practitioners, and conservation organizations
Additional Information:

To be considered, please submit your application electronically via Workday. Application materials must include: 

Required:
Cover letter- Describe your qualifications, area(s) of expertise, career goals, and alignment with desired qualifications and preferred qualifications where applicable
Curriculum Vita (CV)
Statement of Teaching and Mentoring (no more than 2 pages)
Statement of Service/Outreach (no more than 2 pages)
Names/contact information of three references ( Note: Letters of reference are expected to be solicited prior to advancing to the next stage of the hiring process; inform your references when you apply so that letters can be finalized at/soon after time of request )

Initial consideration will be given to applications received by Friday November 16, 2026. Review of applications will continue until the position has been filled. We welcome informal inquiries, which can be made by contacting Search Committee Chair Dr. Chris Tonra at [email removed].

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Ithaca, New York.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: Under guidance of the mentor, you will participate in research investigating the use of entomopathogenic fungi for protection of plants against invertebrate pests, including the invasive beetle (emerald ash borer) and nematode (soybean and potato cyst nematodes) pests. A major focus of this project is investigating the role of microbial metabolites and toxins in antagonism of invertebrate pests and developing methods for formulating fungal and bacterial consortia for biocontrol. Training will be provided in sterile culturing of microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) and isolation of microbes from environmental samples. Research will also involve functional bioassays and growth chamber experiments to test biocontrol efficacy of fungi and microbial consortia against invertebrate pests and isolation of DNA and RNA for genome and transcriptome sequencing to understand mechanisms of antagonism of microbes against invertebrate pests.

Learn how entomopathogenic fungi and microbial communities can be used as biological controls for plant-damaging invertebrate pests.
Gain knowledge of invasive and agricultural pests, including emerald ash borer and soybean and potato cyst nematodes.
Develop sterile laboratory culturing skills for bacteria and fungi.
Gain hands-on experience isolating microorganisms from environmental samples and maintaining microbial cultures.
Learn how microbial metabolites and toxins contribute to antagonism against insect and nematode pests.
Develop familiarity with formulating fungal and bacterial consortia for practical biocontrol applications.
Gain experience conducting functional bioassays and growth-chamber experiments to evaluate biocontrol effectiveness.
Learn to collect, isolate, and prepare DNA and RNA samples for genome and transcriptome sequencing.
Develop an understanding of how genomic and transcriptomic data can be used to investigate microbial mechanisms of pest antagonism.

Lab: The Nancy Fair Link Laminitis Research Center at the Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine is dedicated to improving the prevention, diagnosis and management of equine laminitis. The Center benefits from a collaborative environment that bridges fundamental research and clinical application. It is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities to support research across the full spectrum of laminitis: from the molecular mechanisms to the development of new diagnostic tools and management strategies.

Project:  Insulin dysregulation is an endocrine disease resulting in hyperinsulinemia and is a major risk factor for endocrinopathic laminitis. How different tissues adapt metabolically or contribute to this condition remains poorly understood. The postdoctoral researcher will lead the ex vivo metabolic characterization of key insulin-responsive and laminitis-relevant tissues. The project will combine primary cell models with tissue-level approaches (precision-cut tissue slices, tissue explants, high-resolution respirometry, extracellular flux analysis and stable isotope tracing) to describe insulin signaling and energy metabolism across tissues. The successful candidate will have the opportunity to shape the scientific direction of the project, develop independent research questions within it, and contribute to the supervision of graduate students.

Profile: Applicants must hold a PhD (or be close to completion) in Biology, Physiology, Biochemistry, Veterinary Science or a related discipline. Candidates should have a strong background in cellular or tissue metabolism and hands-on experience with at least one ex vivo approach, such as primary cell isolation and culture, tissue explant or slice models, or mitochondrial function assays. Experience with metabolic flux or respirometry techniques, molecular analysis of insulin signaling, or omics data analysis is a plus. A track record of first-author publications, good written and spoken communication in English, and the ability to work both independently and as part of an interdisciplinary team are expected. Prior experience with equine or large-animal research is not required.

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW!


WDFW’s Fish Ageing and Otolith Laboratories provide critical age and origin data to WDFW Fish Management and Hatchery Divisions, tribal co-managers, and federal fisheries managers to be used in forecasting, run reconstruction, stock assessment, and scientific research.

With your expertise in the preparation and processing of calcified structures, you will conduct research and report on biological studies of Pacific Salmon and other marine, anadromous, and freshwater fishes.

Your work as part of the Otolith Laboratory Team will directly support efforts to meet resource and economic needs for the State of Washington and the Pacific Northwest, including programs focused on recovering Endangered Species Act (ESA) sensitive stocks.


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Otolith Laboratory Biologist’s duties will include,

Thermal Mark Implementation and Evaluation:
Prepare high-quality, half-sectioned and thin-sectioned otolith samples.
Use lapping wheels for grinding and polishing.
Communicate effectively with lab team members and supervisor to ensure accuracy and meet project deadlines.
Independently observe otoliths using compound and dissecting microscopes to identify and decode thermal marks.
Accurately records thermal mark information into database.
Review and plan distinctive thermal mark patterns aligned with hatchery requests.
Develop thermal marking schedules.
Coordinate, adapt, and communicate hatchery thermal marking schedules to achieve intended thermal marks.

Microstructural and Microchemical Analyses:
Prepare high-quality samples from otoliths and other calcified structures for microstructural and microchemical analyses using low-speed saws and lapping wheels.
Use image analysis software and microscopes to measure and count daily increments in otoliths to evaluate environmental, ecological, and anthropogenic influences on growth during early life history.
Evaluate and summarize results of daily growth estimates, accuracy and precision of estimates, size-at-marine entry, and other relevant parameters.

Data Collection, Analysis, and Reporting:
Perform statistical analysis and interpretation of data.
Prepare reports, peer-reviewed publications, and presentations at conferences and other meetings.

Assisting and Supporting Production, Thermal Marking Operations, and Field Collections:
Assist hatchery and lab staff with artificially spawning and cross-fertilizing salmonid gametes.
Travel to study sites to assist with or lead collection efforts for biological samples.

 Working Conditions:

Work Setting, including hazards: Work primarily occurs in a laboratory setting, but will also include office environments, hatcheries, and field sites. Perform repetitive fine motor functions for long durations. Extended periods of time will be spent looking at computer monitors or through microscopes.

Laboratory hazards include hot surfaces (hot plates, burners), grinding wheels, sharp blades, dissecting tools, and chemical exposure (acids, ethanol, acetone, thermoplastic resin, and polystyrene resin) both direct and as fumes.

Hatchery and field work may be performed during inclement weather and over slippery, uneven terrain near or on the water. Lift equipment, samples, coolers, and field gear weighing up to 75 pounds, with assistance as needed. Travel will include operating, or being a passenger in, a motor vehicle on highways or dirt roads. This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule: Typically, Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. The work schedule may require weekend work or extended hours while in the field.

Travel Requirements: Occasional field work, laboratory work, and projects will require travel throughout Washington state. Attend annual workshops and conferences. Travel may include overnight and day trips. Increased travel potential November–February.

Tools and Equipment: Compound and dissecting (stereo) microscopes, epifluorescence microscope, desktop/laptop computers, image analysis software, dissecting tools, precision grinders, hot plates, fume hood, balances, and low-speed precision saws will be used routinely. Portable chilling units and pumps will occasionally be set up and maintained for hatchery production or controlled experiments.

Customer Interactions: Public interactions are uncommon but may occur when entering state buildings, working at hatcheries, or conducting fieldwork. Collaborate and professionally communicate with Tribal/First Nation groups and co-managers, WDFW staff throughout the state, non-profit organizations, academic groups, public utilities, federal agencies, other Washington state resource agencies, and fisheries agencies from other states.


Qualifications:

Closely related qualifying experience may be substituted for the required education on a year-by-year basis.

Required Qualifications:

Option 1:
A Bachelor's degree in fisheries, biology, natural resource science, environmental science, or a related field.
  AND
Three (3) years of professional experience in fish research or management.

Option 2:
Two (2) years as a Fish & Wildlife Biologist 2.


In addition to meeting one of the options listed above, the following are also required and may be gained concurrently:

One (1) year of experience with the following:
Processing or analyzing calcified structures.
Producing high-quality otolith sections, including preparing and analyzing otoliths for thermal mark interrogations, microstructure, and/or microchemistry analysis.
Reading and interpreting multiple band otolith patterns, including reading/evaluating calcified structures for age estimation or thermal mark patterns.

Ability to:
Accurately perform repetitive motions utilizing fine motor skills for long periods of time.
Prepare 20-40 otolith thin sections and 50-100 otolith half sections daily.
Read 100-300 otolith samples daily.

Knowledge of:
Pacific salmon life history and growth.


Please Note:
A Master’s degree in the applicable science may substitute for one (1) year of the required experience in fish research or management.
A Ph.D. in the applicable science may substitute for two (2) years of the required experience in fish research or management.

Valid Driver’s License.


Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess some or all the following:

Master’s degree in a relevant biological science.

Experience:
Processing and analyzing data obtained from otoliths or other calcified structures.
Applying current fish ageing research methods.
Enumerating daily growth increments in otoliths.
Otolith thermal mark identification.
With, or knowledge of, Pacific Northwest fish biology and ecology, including life history and population dynamics.
Managing multiple complex projects with competing deadlines, producing accurate and timely work.
Analyzing data to evaluate issues, assess options, draw conclusions, and support decision-making.

Assistant Professor in Aquatic Ecosystem Ecology


The Department of Zoology and Physiology at the University of Wyoming invites applications for a tenure-track position in Aquatic Ecosystem Ecology at the rank of Assistant Professor. We seek an innovative scientist who will establish an extramurally-funded research program addressing fundamental and/or applied questions in freshwater ecosystem ecology. We particularly welcome candidates whose research examines how aquatic ecosystems respond to environmental change and whose work connects ecological processes across organisms, communities, ecosystems, and watersheds.


The successful candidate will join a highly collaborative community of UW-based ecologists, hydrologists, environmental scientists, and natural-resource scientists working across Wyoming and the broader Rocky Mountain region. Potential areas of research include, but are not limited to: biogeochemistry and elemental cycling, aquatic-terrestrial linkages, water quality, food-web dynamics, and ecosystem responses to anthropogenic disturbances (e.g., climate change, land-use, invasive species, and eutrophication) in stream and lake ecosystems. Research that complements and expands existing strengths at UW and that integrates field experimentation, long-term ecological observation, quantitative approaches, modeling, remote sensing, molecular or isotopic techniques, or other innovative approaches is encouraged.


The University of Wyoming provides exceptional opportunities for aquatic ecosystem research with world-class facilities, including the Red Buttes Environmental Laboratory, a research laboratory specifically designed for aquatic research, the University of Wyoming Stable Isotope Facility, and the AMK Ranch, a field station operated in collaboration with Grand Teton National Park. The University of Wyoming also provides nearby access to lakes, reservoirs, rivers, wetlands, and watersheds across elevational gradients throughout the Rocky Mountain West. The successful candidate will be expected to develop a nationally-recognized, extramurally funded research program, mentor graduate and undergraduate students and conduct research within a diverse dynamic department spanning from neurobiology to ecology and wildlife management, and participate in the Program in Ecology and Evolution and other relevant interdisciplinary programs and initiatives. 


The successful candidate will also contribute to undergraduate and graduate education. Teaching responsibilities may include courses in aquatic ecology, ecosystem ecology, ecology, environmental science, quantitative ecology, or related areas, depending on the candidate's expertise and departmental needs. Candidates are expected to demonstrate a commitment to inclusive, evidence-based teaching and effective mentoring of students from diverse backgrounds.

Candidates must have a Ph.D. in ecology, biology, aquatic science, environmental science, limnology, hydrology, or a closely related field, research expertise in ecosystem ecology, biogeochemistry, or a closely related field in freshwater systems, and evidence of scholarly productivity appropriate to the career stage.

Located in Laramie, Wyoming, UW provides direct access to an exceptional natural laboratory spanning high-elevation alpine and subalpine systems, streams and rivers, lakes and reservoirs, and diverse watersheds of the Rocky Mountain West. The university's location creates outstanding opportunities for field-based research addressing aquatic ecosystem responses to climate variability, land-use change, resource development, and other environmental pressures. ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Pacific West Area (PWA) at the Temperate Tree Fruit and Vegetable Research Unit located in Wapato, Washington.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The unit focuses on developing novel biological, molecular, and bio-intensive methods to control insect pests and plant pathogens affecting temperate tree fruits (apples, pears, and stone fruits like sweet cherries) and vegetable crops. 

For more information on the agency, visit the USDA Agricultural Research Service Home Page.

Research Project: You will engage in a collaborative research initiative focused on evaluating therapeutic interventions against Cherry X-disease (Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni), a major threat to sweet cherry and stone fruit production in the Pacific Northwest.

Under the mentorship of USDA-ARS research scientists, you will gain hands-on experience utilizing an in vitroplant tissue culture and molecular screening platform to evaluate candidate therapeutic compounds (such as EPA-registered antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, or biologically active molecules) for their efficacy in suppressing phytoplasma titers.

Learning Objectives: Throughout this educational fellowship, you will have opportunities to receive training and gain practical experience in:

Micropropagation & Plant Tissue Culture: Participating in the maintenance, subculturing, and propagation of micropropagated in vitro cherry plantlet culture systems under sterile laboratory conditions.

Therapeutic Application & Assay Setup: Learning and applying protocols to incorporate test therapeutics into plantlet growth media or application systems to evaluate compound uptake and plant physiological responses.

Molecular Diagnostics & Quantification: Collecting plant tissue samples and performing molecular diagnostic assays, including DNA/RNA extractions, end-point PCR, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), and reverse transcription qPCR (RT-qPCR) to quantify pathogen dynamics and gene expression.

Data Analysis & Synthesis: Learning to process, analyze, and interpret diagnostic dataset outputs using statistical tools and software to compare treatment efficacy and phytoplasma titer reductions over time.

Scientific Communication & Collaboration: Collaborating with interdisciplinary research teams, presenting findings during internal research updates, and contributing data synthesis for peer-reviewed journal articles, conference presentations, and technical reports.

This opportunity is designed to enhance your professional and technical skills in molecular plant pathology, bio-assay design, and sustainable crop protection methodologies in alignment with the scientific mission of the USDA-ARS.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

Applying computational pipelines, bioinformatic approaches, statistical analyses, and quality assurance/quality control principles to complex biological data sets including those from next generation sequencing-based technologies.
Compiling and summarizing scientific information from the peer-reviewed literature and from on-line data sources.
Extracting biomolecules such as RNA and DNA from animal tissues.
Developing methods to edit genome using CRISPR-based systems

Description
Help restore Iowa’s natural beauty while learning about ecology, land management and wildlife as land stewardship intern! As an INHF intern, you’ll be part of one of the most respected internship programs in the state.

Internship description
Land stewardship interns work hard to maintain and restore native landscapes across Iowa in four distinct regions: Central Iowa, Eastern Iowa, Loess Hills, Lakes Area and the Blufflands. A crew is hired each summer for each region; see the region descriptions below for specifics. 

Interns will conduct needed land management and restoration on remnant and reconstructed prairies, woodlands, oak savannas and other natural areas owned or protected by INHF. Interns will use a variety of hand tools and chainsaws to help accomplish restoration goals. 

Interns will learn from and work closely with landowners and working professionals in the field. Educational opportunities, including participation in regional conferences, will be provided. 

The internship will give interns vital skills and experience for a career in conservation or land management, as well as a greater appreciation for the importance of our natural areas. It meets most college credit requirements for work/internship experience. This is a physically demanding, yet very rewarding internship.

Work examples
Much of the work will focus on prairie, oak savanna and woodland restoration with an emphasis on invasive species control. Control of species is by chainsaw, hand saw, digging, pulling and herbicide treatment. Specifically, interns may be:

Mechanically removing eastern red cedars and other woody species from prairies and woodlands
Hand pulling invasive species like wild parsnip and sweet clover from prairies
Stream bank stabilization, fire break construction, wildlife habitat management and prairie seed collection are other possible intern activities
INHF's land internship program prioritizes safety. All interns will receive training in the chainsaw/brush saw operation, UTV operation, herbicide application, first aid and CPR and workplace harassment prevention.

Skills/Qualifications
This internship is physically demanding, requiring fit, motivated individuals. Those with a positive attitude, eagerness to learn and desire to make our natural areas healthier are well-suited for this position. Interns will work exclusively outdoors in all kinds of weather conditions including heat, humidity and rain. 

Driving to various work sites and occasional camping (amount of camping varies by region; see specific details in the regional breakdown) is required. Interns must have a working vehicle or be able to coordinate a ride or carpool. 

College students of any age, even freshmen and graduate students, are eligible to apply. Compatible majors to this internship include, but are not limited to: animal ecology, botany, biology, forestry, environmental studies or environmental science. 

Applicants, except those applying for a position in the Loess Hills region, must have an Iowa connection (a family relation, attending an Iowa school or be originally from Iowa, for example).

Regional Crew Details
INHF stewardship staff work across the state in five different regions; currently, interns are hired in the Central, Eastern, Loess Hills, Lakes Area and Blufflands regions. Learn about the specifics for each regional internship below. 

Central:
Work areas include around 20 different sites in the Central Region; much of the work occurs near Des Moines with headquarters at Snyder Heritage Farm in Elkhart
Typically hire 6-7 interns
Housing is available in this region
Interns camp 5-6 weeks of the 11-week term in state/county parks and public natural areas; meals are provided while interns are camping
For more information, contact Derek Miner, land stewardship associate at [email removed] or 515-288-1846, ext. 17.

Eastern:
Work sites are predominately within a 12-county area, with an emphasis in Iowa, Johnson and Scott counties with headquarters at Kahler Prairie, just outside of Iowa City 
Typically hire 3 interns
Housing is not offered for this region
Limited camping will be required; meals are provided during camping times
For more information, contact Bill Kohler, eastern Iowa land stewardship director, at [email removed] or (515) 809-5681.

Loess Hills:
Work sites are predominately within a 13-county area, with an emphasis in Monona and Harrison counties with headquarters near Pisgah; regular work on steep, hilly terrain
Typically hire 3 interns
Housing may be available for this position
Limited camping will be required when working outside of Loess Hills region; meals are provided during camping times
Applicants do not need to have an Iowa connection to apply
For more information, contact Kody Wohlers, Loess Hills land stewardship director, at [email removed] or 402-578-1935.

Lakes Area:
Work sites are predominately within a 17-county area, with an emphasis in Dickinson and Kossuth counties. 
Typically hire 2 interns
Housing may be available for this position
Limited camping will occur if working outside of the region; meals are provided during camping times
For more information contact Tanner Bouchard, lakes area land stewardship director, at [email removed].

Blufflands:
Work sites are predominately within a 7-county area, with an emphasis in Winneshiek and Allamakee counties with headquarters in Decorah; regular work on steep, hilly terrain
Typically hire 5-6 interns
Housing is not offered for this region
Limited camping will occur if working outside of the Blufflands region; meals are provided during camping times
For more information contact Jered Bourquin, blufflands associate, at  [email removed] or 563-382-2008.


Hours and Compensation
Internship begins May 17 and ends August 5. Interns will work a total of 11 weeks within that period; the week of the 4th of July is off. The work week will consist of 10-hour days, Monday through Thursday. Compensation is $15/hr.
